[{:db/id 17592186100923 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5a60deb5-551b-564a-a9a5-424f5c35cb79" "question-35ba1238-9d03-56c3-a9e7-b912f69594b6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100922 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-026fc717-7ff3-5e33-aea2-f16023ff29e1" "question-abf79c71-49dc-5540-8e88-cbf4204858e9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-5a60deb5-551b-564a-a9a5-424f5c35cb79" :question/id #uuid "5a60deb5-551b-564a-a9a5-424f5c35cb79" :question/math-academy-id "q-17554" :question/problem "Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{{z}^{-1}({z}^{-1}-1)}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{z({z}^{-1}-1)}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1-z}{x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1-z}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{z}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ x\frac{dz}{dx}+z & =1 \\ \frac{d}{dx}(zx) & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(zx)\,dx & =\int 1\,dx \\ zx & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{x+C}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fc48d748-c473-5089-bb17-fc3ad8129f55"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fc48d748-c473-5089-bb17-fc3ad8129f55" :answer-field/id #uuid "fc48d748-c473-5089-bb17-fc3ad8129f55" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-cde43acc-0b98-5113-aa21-f90fd88d5eb9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-07e8f688-4e1e-5c56-97f0-ebcb8599d2bf" "answer-b4d45c86-e566-5b1e-8a2b-c81f4e145b01" "answer-67100b80-0a22-513b-a893-f811e8dbb561" "answer-ef914b0e-cc6b-5a2c-bbbd-fc5145c04181" "answer-cde43acc-0b98-5113-aa21-f90fd88d5eb9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07e8f688-4e1e-5c56-97f0-ebcb8599d2bf" :answer/id #uuid "07e8f688-4e1e-5c56-97f0-ebcb8599d2bf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=-\frac{1}{x+C}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b4d45c86-e566-5b1e-8a2b-c81f4e145b01" :answer/id #uuid "b4d45c86-e566-5b1e-8a2b-c81f4e145b01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{-1+Cx}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-67100b80-0a22-513b-a893-f811e8dbb561" :answer/id #uuid "67100b80-0a22-513b-a893-f811e8dbb561" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{1+Cx}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef914b0e-cc6b-5a2c-bbbd-fc5145c04181" :answer/id #uuid "ef914b0e-cc6b-5a2c-bbbd-fc5145c04181" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{1+C{e}^{x}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cde43acc-0b98-5113-aa21-f90fd88d5eb9" :answer/id #uuid "cde43acc-0b98-5113-aa21-f90fd88d5eb9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{x+C}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-35ba1238-9d03-56c3-a9e7-b912f69594b6" :question/id #uuid "35ba1238-9d03-56c3-a9e7-b912f69594b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-168136" :question/problem "Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-y\,,\,x>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/3}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z & =\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{x}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{3}} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{x} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}z & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z] & =3{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z]\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3}z & ={x}^{3}+C \\ z & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}},\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5a6c67e1-0333-5cc2-869a-1bbcb67a5ad4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z=3{x}^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1/2}.$*" :question/worked-solution "The substitution $z={y}^{-1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z=3{x}^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(1)={(\frac{1}{9})}^{-1/2}=3\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=3{x}^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2\int 1/x\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-2}} \\  & ={x}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{-2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\,z & =3 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z & =3x+C \\ z & =3{x}^{3}+C{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(1)=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(1) & =3 \\ 3(1)^{3}+C(1)^{2} & =3 \\ 3+C & =3 \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=3{x}^{3}\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{-1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1/2} & =z \\ {y}^{-1/2} & =3{x}^{3} \\ {y}^{1/2} & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9{x}^{6}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8efc61ad-4fda-52b5-938e-e4876d1543c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*" :question/worked-solution "The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C \\ z & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition  $y(1)=\frac{1}{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+C} \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{1}{0+C} \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0c2ae4a2-7aee-5a15-87d2-14ca2c8d362a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0c2ae4a2-7aee-5a15-87d2-14ca2c8d362a" :answer-field/id #uuid "0c2ae4a2-7aee-5a15-87d2-14ca2c8d362a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c089f48e-5eec-5164-9b80-a61e10c8f30b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5ce1a23c-a543-5a3a-976c-513bed73760b" "answer-d310da97-f3cf-5dae-870e-04cfe0711dde" "answer-3d4e3eb2-e031-5967-901f-7f694c829795" "answer-c089f48e-5eec-5164-9b80-a61e10c8f30b" "answer-b9618fff-b0d5-5622-add2-f2d1be8efb58"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ce1a23c-a543-5a3a-976c-513bed73760b" :answer/id #uuid "5ce1a23c-a543-5a3a-976c-513bed73760b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2}{6x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d310da97-f3cf-5dae-870e-04cfe0711dde" :answer/id #uuid "d310da97-f3cf-5dae-870e-04cfe0711dde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+3}{9{x}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3d4e3eb2-e031-5967-901f-7f694c829795" :answer/id #uuid "3d4e3eb2-e031-5967-901f-7f694c829795" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c089f48e-5eec-5164-9b80-a61e10c8f30b" :answer/id #uuid "c089f48e-5eec-5164-9b80-a61e10c8f30b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9618fff-b0d5-5622-add2-f2d1be8efb58" :answer/id #uuid "b9618fff-b0d5-5622-add2-f2d1be8efb58" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101031 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

:question/problem "Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-y\,,\,x>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{3}.$*"] ["question-35ba1238-9d03-56c3-a9e7-b912f69594b6" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/3}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z & =\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{x}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{3}} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{x} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}z & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z] & =3{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z]\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3}z & ={x}^{3}+C \\ z & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}},\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-35ba1238-9d03-56c3-a9e7-b912f69594b6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5a6c67e1-0333-5cc2-869a-1bbcb67a5ad4" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
xe^y\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}+e^y = e^{x} \, ,

given that $y(1)=1$ and $x>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's make a substitution

$$
z=e^y\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get $\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}=e^y\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of  $z$ as follows:

$$
x\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}+z=e^x\,,
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(1)=e^{y(1)}=e^1=e\,.
$$

Notice that the left-hand side of the differential equation is now an exact derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & ={e}^{x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\text{d}x \\ xz & ={e}^{x}+C \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{x}+C}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(1)=e\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(1) & =e \\ \frac{{e}^{1}+C}{1} & =e \\ e+C & =e \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z  =   \frac{e^x}{x}\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=e^y.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y} & =z \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{x} \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{x}}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\  & =x-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,,\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$ So, the final solution is

$$
y = x - \ln (x), \quad x > 0.

:question/problem "Find the general solution to the following first-order ODE using the substitution $z=y^3.$

$$
xy^2\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = x^2+y^3
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's make a substitution

$$
z=y^3\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}=3y^2\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^2\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

 Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{3}\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}\right)=x^2+z
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3}{x}({x}^{2}+z) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3x+\frac{3}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=3x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3x \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,z & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}}) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\ \frac{z}{{x}^{3}} & =-\frac{3}{x}+C \\ z & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=y^3.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =z \\ {y}^{3} & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048569} {:db/id 17592186101247 :question/id #uuid "ffe3c5eb-c32b-557c-96a7-7ea03bab3fa8" :question/math-academy-id "q-17544"} {:db/id 17592186101249 :question/id #uuid differential equation

$$
2y\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}+y^2=x.
$$

Notice that it is *not* a first-order linear equation because it cannot be written in the form $y' + P(x) y = Q(x).$ In fact, this equation is an example of a *nonlinear* first-order differential equation.

We can sometimes transform a nonlinear differential equation into a linear differential equation using a substitution. If we can do this, then we can apply the method of integrating factors to solve it.

To transform the above equation into a linear differential equation, we can use the substitution

$$
z=y^2.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}z} {\textrm{d}x}=2y\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}z} {\textrm{d}x}+z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear! So, we can use the method of integrating factors. The given equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=x.$ We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=e^x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}{e}^{x}+z{e}^{x} & =x{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =x{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now integrate with respect to $x,$ using integration by parts to integrate the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{x}\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =(x-1){e}^{x}+C \\ z & =x-1+C{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=y^2.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =z \\ {y}^{2} & =x-1+C{e}^{-x} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{x-1+C{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60bfb242-6329-5820-adf6-d96d5c970d57" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4060 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caa22dea-6722-5c27-aa99-c035d6beef32" :step/math-academy-id
